title: Callaloo
subtitle: caribbean coconut and leafy greens stew
excerpt: Callaloo is a rich Caribbean stew of dark leafy greens cooked in coconut milk with okra, scotch bonnet and thyme until thick and deeply flavoured. Serves 4 as a side.
sourceNotes: Callaloo is the national dish of Trinidad and Tobago and is central to the cooking of many Caribbean islands. The name refers both to the dish and the leafy green used to make it.

glossaryTerms.definition: A Caribbean leafy green stew made from taro leaves or amaranth, rich with coconut milk.
A green pod vegetable that releases a natural thickener when cooked, giving callaloo its body.

content.text: thickens itself naturally as it cooks.
releases a viscous liquid that binds the stew as it simmers, while the callaloo leaves collapse into the coconut milk to create a deep green, silky dish. No flour or other thickener is needed.

Callaloo leaves can be found at Caribbean and African grocery shops. Spinach makes a reasonable substitute but lacks the slightly earthy depth of taro or dasheen leaves. The scotch bonnet should be kept whole unless you want significant heat in every mouthful.
Heat the oil in the large saucepan over medium heat. Fry the onion, garlic and spring onion for 5 minutes until softened.
Add the callaloo leaves in batches, stirring as each batch wilts down. Add the thyme and whole scotch bonnet.
Pour in the coconut milk and add the sliced okra. Stir to combine.
Simmer over medium-low heat for 15 to 20 minutes until the leaves are completely tender, the okra has softened and the stew has thickened.
Remove the scotch bonnet and thyme. Season to taste. Serve as a side dish with rice, or as part of a larger Caribbean spread.

attrs.problem: The callaloo is very thin and watery.
attrs.solution: The okra may not have released its natural thickener yet. Continue simmering uncovered for 5 to 10 more minutes. Alternatively, add a little more okra.

attrs.problem: The scotch bonnet burst and the callaloo is very spicy.
attrs.solution: Remove it immediately and taste. If too hot, a splash of coconut milk can help calm the heat slightly. Keep the bonnet whole next time.

attrs.problem: The colour is dull and khaki rather than bright green.
attrs.solution: The leaves were cooked too long or at too high a heat. Callaloo will darken some, but a vivid green at the start helps. Do not cover the pot during simmering.

content.text: Callaloo is the national dish of Trinidad and Tobago, eaten at Sunday lunch and special occasions. In Jamaica a similar dish is made from ackee leaves or spinach. Across the Eastern Caribbean it appears at every celebration table. It is a side dish that often ends up as the most popular thing at the table.
